vectors.description: flag.type arrives as 0 instead of "Boolean" (the #2279 shape) -> reject wholesale
flag.fallthrough.type arrives as 0 instead of "Fixed" -> reject wholesale
segment.conditionLogic arrives as 0 instead of "And" -> reject wholesale. Ordinal 0 is And and 1 is Or, so silently accepting flips a segment between matching ALL of its conditions and ANY of them
segment.conditions[].operator arrives as 0 instead of "Equals" -> reject wholesale
rule.conditionGroups[].operator arrives as 0 instead of "And" -> reject wholesale

An UNRECOGNISED condition operator NAME is accepted, not rejected: that is how a newer server ships a new operator, and the evaluator fails it closed (#2262/#2372). Carries a flag as well as the segment: php's last-known-good guard keys off an empty flag list

An UNRECOGNISED flag type NAME is accepted, not rejected (#2395). Same forward-compatibility rule as the operator above, but on stronger ground: NOTHING evaluates flag.type. It is parsed, stored and never read, and go/ruby/php do not model the field at all -- so rejecting it failed the ENTIRE fetch over a field no evaluator consults, and the day a new flag type ships every pinned SDK would stop serving EVERY flag. The unknown type sits on the accepted flag itself, so asserting the flag is present proves it was RETAINED, not merely that the payload parsed. Deliberately not extended to serve.type or conditionLogic: those ARE consulted, and each dispatches on a two-way branch that would silently take the else arm (rollout / OR) rather than fail -- they need an entity-level drop instead, which is the follow-up to #2395
Unknown properties from a newer server are ignored, not rejected

An UNRECOGNISED serve type NAME on flag.fallthrough drops THAT FLAG and nothing else (#2402). Unlike flag.type this field IS consulted, and every evaluator dispatches on a two-way branch -- `serve.type == "Fixed"` else ROLLOUT -- so tolerating the value the way #2395 tolerates an unknown flag type would bucket the flag against weights that may not exist, silently, instead of failing. Rejecting the whole payload is equally wrong: an additive server change would take down every flag on a pinned client. Dropping the containing flag routes the caller through the FlagNotFound path every SDK already implements -- their default for exactly the affected flag -- and leaves the rest serving

The same unrecognised serve type, this time on a RULE's serve rather than the fallthrough. Carried separately because the two are parsed at different depths and an implementation that guards only the fallthrough looks correct against the vector above while still mis-serving every rule match (#2402)

An UNRECOGNISED conditionLogic NAME on a SEGMENT drops that segment, keeping every flag -- including one whose rule POINTS AT the dropped segment (#2402). This is the serious half of the defect: `logic == "And"` else ANY means an unrecognised value makes a segment meant to require ALL of its conditions match ANY of them, so the rule fails OPEN and over-targets. `mc-references-dropped-segment` is retained deliberately -- the drop is scoped to the entity that carried the bad value, and a naive implementation that walked the reference and dropped the flag too would fail here. What happens to that dangling reference at EVALUATION time is pinned separately and engine-generated, by the `f-segment-unresolvable` flagVector: every evaluator already treats an unresolvable segmentKey as no-match, so the cascade fails CLOSED

The same unrecognised conditionLogic NAME, this time as a rule condition GROUP's operator. Same enum, different carrier: the group lives on a flag rather than a segment, so the entity dropped is the FLAG. Carried separately because an implementation that guards segment.conditionLogic alone still lets a group operator fall through to the OR arm and over-target (#2402)
